bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Input-cost volatility, concentrated in Edible Oils — MD&A: 'the business continues to remain exposed to volatility in input costs, particularly within the Edible Oils segment.' Crude sunflower oil prices rose by over 10% during FY'26 and management flags that 'The recent uptick in crude-linked input costs poses a potential headwind to margins going forward.' Explicitly structural rather than transient: 'While the contribution of the Edible Oils business to the overall portfolio has reduced over time, it continues to have a sensitivity for the Company's overall profitability.' Mitigation stated as portfolio diversification, calibrated pricing actions and continued scale-up of the higher-margin Foods business.
- Price-elasticity of demand — passing on inflation costs volume — MD&A: 'Inflationary pressures in key raw materials have the potential to impact margins and necessitate price increases, which may in turn affect consumption.' Demonstrated in-year rather than hypothetical: in Premium Staples the Company 'successfully passed on the increase in input costs' but 'higher pricing had an impact on volumes during the year' (volume +2% against value +16%, largely price-driven), and category gross margins still declined 9%.
- Competitive intensity and share loss in Spreads & Dips — MD&A: heightened competitive intensity during FY'26 'particularly in Organised and Standalone Modern Trade (SAMT), with sustained pricing pressure', intensified by 'the entry and rapid scale-up of new-age brands, which gained share across e-commerce and modern trade channels through premium offerings such as high-protein and chocolate variants.' The category registered a volume decline of 10% and a value decline of 7% during the year — the only core Foods category in outright decline other than the deliberately-exited Chocolates.
- GHG emissions and climate-transition exposure across a processing-intensive plant base — BRSR material-issues table, row 1 (classified RISK): 'Sundrop Brands' operates six manufacturing plants across climate-vulnerable regions. Processing-intensive operations generate significant Scope 1 and 2 emissions. BRSR Core reasonable assurance became mandatory for top 1,000 companies in FY25-26, requiring verified GHG accounting. India's net-zero 2070 commitment creates investor scrutiny on decarbonization. Failure to demonstrate emission reduction could impact access to green financing.' Stated negative implications: transition costs for renewable installations, efficiency upgrades and carbon accounting systems, plus 'Potential carbon tax liability if pricing mechanisms implemented.'
- Acute water stress at plant locations — licence-to-operate and shutdown risk — BRSR row 3 (RISK): 'Sundrop Brands' plants in Gujarat, Telangana, and UP face acute water stress. Gujarat's central-east region experiences severe drought. Telangana's groundwater crisis deepens—study by Telangana Rythu Commission and University of Hyderabad (January 2026) warns of Day Zero threat by 2034 with groundwater levels projected to decline 68%. Edible oil refining and food processing are water-intensive. Communities surrounding plants compete for scarce groundwater. Regulatory authorities tightened abstraction permits in FY25-26.' Stated negative implication includes 'Risk of production shutdowns if permits suspended' plus capital investment for ZLD systems, water recycling infrastructure and rainwater harvesting.
- Employee health & safety across high-temperature and chemical-handling operations — BRSR row 5 (RISK): 'Six facilities with diverse processes—oil refining at high temperatures, automated packaging, chemical handling—expose workers to heat stress, machinery accidents, and chemical hazards. Summer 2025 saw record temperatures in Gujarat and Telangana. Assam plant faces recurring monsoon floods. OSH Code implementation progresses at state level, raising compliance standards. BRSR Core mandates LTIFR disclosure with reasonable assurance.' Stated negatives include potential liabilities from workplace accidents including compensation and legal costs.
- Human-rights and labour-rights exposure in an MSME/smallholder agricultural supply chain — BRSR row 6 (RISK): 'Sundrop Brands' procures from MSMEs and small producers (24% direct procurement per FY25 and 25% per FY26), creating exposure to labour rights risks in agricultural supply chains—particularly peanut sourcing in Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh. Seasonal agricultural workers from marginalized communities face wage violations and unsafe conditions. India's ILO convention ratification and emerging global supply chain due diligence standards create rising scrutiny. Inadequate grievance mechanisms could trigger ESG index exclusions.' Compounding this, the Company states it has no formal supplier awareness programme yet (see esg list) — a supplier-oversight gap against an identified supply-chain risk.
- Labour practices — wages, peak-season hours, unionisation and low gender diversity — BRSR row 7 (RISK): 'Food processing faces scrutiny over fair wages, working hours during peak seasons, and freedom of association. Telangana and Gujarat plants face unionization pressures. Gender diversity remains low in manufacturing. Labour' — the rationale cell TRUNCATES mid-sentence at the word 'Labour' and its mitigation column is split across a page break, surviving only as 'Conducting living wage gap analysis benchmarking against credible methodologies for all locations. Ensuring compliance with'. Stated negatives: incremental cost for wage-gap bridging, enhanced benefits and HR system upgrades.
- Climate vulnerability of agricultural sourcing (raw-material availability and price) — BRSR row 8 (RISK): 'Sundrop Brands' agricultural sourcing faces acute climate vulnerability. Assam sources from flood-prone regions—2025 witnessed severe flooding affecting 20+ districts. Gujarat peanut sourcing exposed to intensifying heat and drought—summer 2025 exceeded historical averages. Vegetable supply affected by extreme weather causing persistent volatility. UN ESC' — the row TRUNCATES here at the very end of the routed text, so this risk's mitigation approach and its positive/negative implications are entirely LOST and could not be extracted.
- Structural concentration: single-activity business and a promoter stake wholly under encumbrance — Concentration disclosures that are structural risks though not labelled as such. (a) BRSR Section A states the main activity FMCG accounts for 100% of turnover — no activity diversification outside foods/edible oils. (b) The promoter CAG-Tech (Mauritius) Limited holds 38.91% as at March 31, 2026 and 'the entire shareholding of 1,46,66,522 equity shares ... is subject to encumbrance created by way of Non-Disposal Undertaking as of March 31, 2026' — the whole promoter block is encumbered. (c) FY25 consolidated results are stated to be not comparable to FY26 following the Del Monte Foods Private Limited acquisition, limiting trend readability. [Items (a)-(c) BACK-FILLED with provenance from the sibling profile / strategy_outlook / governance_entities bundles; this risks_esg bundle carries (b) in its own MD&A extract.]

outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Accelerate the transition into a scaled Foods-focused business by continued prioritisation of resources towards proven high-growth and high market share categories (stated Board belief).
- Drive growth through portfolio expansion, distribution scale-up and disciplined brand investments.
- Build on stated leadership in core categories of Ready to Cook and Ready to Eat Popcorn through distribution expansion and entry into smaller towns and rural markets.
- Drive consumption and premiumisation in existing categories through pack upsizing, new innovative flavour and format additions, and by driving both in-home and out-of-home consumption.
- Scale presence in emerging channels — e-commerce and quick commerce — with targeted investments and sharper execution; use E-commerce as a premiumisation vehicle and a testing ground for new launches across core categories (last clause back-filled from the profile bundle, which carries the Future Outlook paragraphs truncated out of this bundle).
- Moderate exposure to the Mass Edible Oils/Staples category deliberately, while protecting absolute margins in the edible oil business.
- Operate the Edible Oil(s) business with volume and margin protection as a key tenet, running regional and select Modern Trade and E-commerce channel-centric experiments to accelerate growth.
- Improve profitability within Premium Staples (Edible Oil) by passing on input-cost increases, and scale adjacencies such as Plain Oats.
- Cease further investments in Chocolates (as aligned with the Board in FY'25) and over time evaluate divesting or re-pivoting capacities in that segment.
- Invest behind brands through digital interventions to strengthen brand salience and drive household penetration; sustain innovation into new segments, formats and taste profiles.
- Mitigate input-cost risk through portfolio diversification, calibrated pricing actions and continued scale-up of the higher-margin Foods business.
- Strengthen the cash position after the Del Monte Foods Private Limited acquisition to pursue organic and inorganic opportunities — capacity expansion as viable, brand development, product innovation and selective strategic acquisitions.
- Drive cost efficiency via multiple initiatives in manufacturing and supply chain to expand margins, with momentum to continue in coming years (back-filled from the profile bundle — this paragraph falls after the truncation point in the strategy_outlook bundle).
- Tech-enable the sales organisation to improve productivity and ROI on channel/trade investments, leveraging the existing sales force automation tool covering approx 3,75,000 outlets (back-filled from the profile bundle for the ROI clause).
- Strengthen competitive positioning in Spreads and Dips through sharper value propositions, improved execution in high-growth channels and calibrated investments to bring back sustainable growth.
- STATED POLICY INTENT (figures deliberately excluded). The Company has adopted a Dividend Distribution Policy pursuant to Regulation 43A of the SEBI Listing Regulations, available on its website. For FY2025-26 the Directors do NOT recommend a dividend, and the Board does not propose to transfer any amount to the General Reserve account. The stated rationale is a growth-oriented capital allocation strategy: following the acquisition of Del Monte Foods Private Limited the Company is 'strengthening its cash position to capitalize on identified high-potential opportunities across both organic and inorganic avenues', specifically 'investments in capacity expansion as viable, brand development, product innovation, and selective strategic acquisitions', and it proposes 'to retain earnings within the business' to fund expansion plans and maintain adequate financial flexibility. [The dividend philosophy is BACK-FILLED with provenance from the sibling profile/strategy_outlook bundles: the section arriving in THIS bundle under the heading '=== DIVIDEND DISTRIBUTION POLICY ===' does not contain a dividend policy at all — see the mismatch note below.] Governance controls over capital and related-party flows: all contracts, arrangements or transactions with related parties during FY2025-26 were in the ordinary course of business and at arm's length, and none was material under the Company's RPT materiality policy; Form AOC-2 is enclosed as Annexure C; related party disclosures including transactions with the Promoter group form part of the Standalone Financial Statements at Note No. 43; a Board-approved Policy on Related Party Transactions (recommended by the Audit Committee) manages conflicts of interest and all RPTs are subject to prior approval/ratification of the Audit Committee. STATED ABSENCE (a real finding): 'No loans/advances in the nature of loans were given by the Company or by its subsidiaries to any firms/companies in which directors are interested during the financial year ended March 31, 2026.' Loans, guarantees and investments under Section 186 are stated to form part of the notes to the financial statements rather than being quantified in the Report. On accounting treatment: 'The Company has complied with the appropriate accounting policies and has ensured that they have been applied consistently. There have been no deviations from the treatment prescribed in the Accounting Standards.' EQUITY-BASED COMPENSATION: the Nomination and Remuneration Committee administers the 'Agro Tech Foods Limited Employees Stock Option Plan, 2024' (the ESOP Scheme 2024), implemented with effect from April 27, 2025; during FY2025-26 the NRC approved grants and forfeitures of Options, the first being a resolution passed by circulation on June 07, 2025 — the number of options granted is NOT recoverable because the text truncates mid-number at 'Approved the grant of 13,8'. AGM: the 39th (Thirty Ninth) Annual General Meeting is to be held on Wednesday, August 26, 2026 at 11.00 AM (IST) through VC/OAVM (date and weekday verified mutually consistent). HEADING/CONTENT MISMATCH: the block labelled '=== DIVIDEND DISTRIBUTION POLICY ===' actually delivers Corporate Governance Report disclosure items (xii) 'Disclosure by listed entity and its subsidiaries of Loans and advances in the nature of loans to firms/companies in which directors are interested by name and amount' and (xiii) 'Disclosure of Accounting Treatment' — it contains no dividend policy, no payout band and no retention philosophy.
- PLANT FOOTPRINT DISCLOSED ONLY HERE (material context for every ESG target below): the BRSR material-issues table states the Company 'operates six manufacturing plants' / 'six facilities', located across Gujarat, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh (UP) and Assam, with agricultural sourcing concentrated in Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh (peanut) and Assam. Note the interaction with the BRSR reporting boundary: the boundary excludes the Krishnapatnam (stated Telangana) and Alwar (Rajasthan) manufacturing facilities because they came into operation mid-year, so 'six' is the in-boundary count and the total operated footprint is not stated as a single number anywhere in the routed text. No capacity figure (MT or TPD) is given for any plant.
- GHG accounting: establishing a Scope 1, 2 and 3 GHG inventory across ALL plants aligned with the GHG Protocol, using FY25-26 as the baseline year.
- Emission-reduction targets: developing science-based emission reduction targets for short-, medium- and long-term, for validation through the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi). Target values and dates are NOT stated.
- Energy efficiency: implementing measures including variable frequency drives, waste heat recovery, and thermal insulation upgrades.
- Renewable energy: initiating renewable energy installations at the Telangana plant (single named site; no MW, no date).
- Logistics decarbonisation: engaging logistics partners on cleaner fuel adoption.
- Assurance: 'Obtaining BRSR Core assurance' is listed as a mitigation, and the same row states 'BRSR Core reasonable assurance became mandatory for top 1,000 companies in FY25-26'. CONTRADICTION FLAGGED — BRSR Section A items 14 and 15 answer 'Whether the company has undertaken reasonable assurance of the BRSR Core? - Not Applicable' and 'Type of Assurance Obtained - Not Applicable'. The Company therefore simultaneously describes BRSR Core assurance as mandatory for its cohort in FY25-26 and reports it as Not Applicable to itself. [Section A items 14-15 BACK-FILLED with provenance from the sibling profile / governance_entities bundles.]
- Water: conducting water risk assessments at the Gujarat, Telangana and UP plants using the WRI Aqueduct tool.
- Water: developing water reduction targets aligned with context-based water stewardship principles, and undertaking process- and application-level water consumption work at the facilities. No numeric reduction target is stated.
- Water: transitioning to dry cleaning and water-efficient systems; upgrading effluent treatment systems toward zero liquid discharge (ZLD) at critical locations; rainwater harvesting.
- Water: engaging communities through watershed management projects and appointing water stewardship champions at each plant.
- Waste (classified an OPPORTUNITY, not a risk): waste-to-value collaborations leveraging the Gujarat and Telangana plants' location in industrial clusters; bio-waste valorization of refining residues; packaging recycling to offset EPR compliance expenses under strengthened EPR regulations mandating demonstrable recycling targets. Mitigation column reads 'Not applicable—this is an opportunity to be pursued'.
- Energy (classified an OPPORTUNITY): renewable energy adoption and efficiency optimisation across the six facilities, supported by India's updated NDCs for 2030, state-level renewable purchase obligations, favourable solar irradiation at the Gujarat and Telangana plants, and declining solar costs. Mitigation column reads 'Not applicable—this is an opportunity to be pursued'.
- Occupational health & safety: developing comprehensive safety management systems aligned with the ISO 45001 framework (alignment stated as an intent — NO ISO 45001 certification is claimed anywhere in the routed text).
- Occupational health & safety: conducting regular HIRA exercises with worker participation; installing/upgrading machine guarding and safety interlocks; addressing heat stress through enhanced ventilation, hydration protocols and work schedule adjustments.
- Occupational health & safety: providing health check-ups to employees AND contractors; establishing occupational health facilities at major plants; conducting safety training in regional languages with competency verification.
- Occupational health & safety: implementing digital incident reporting enabling anonymous near-miss reporting, and constituting safety committees with worker representatives empowered to halt unsafe operations.
- Human rights: developing a Human Rights Policy aligned with the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (stated as under development, i.e. not yet in place).
- Human rights: conducting salient human rights impact assessments at Company-owned and leased premises and gradually extending into high-risk sourcing regions using ILO indicators, prioritising the Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh agricultural clusters.
- Supply chain: implementing a supplier code covering prohibition of child/forced labour, living wages, safe conditions and freedom of association; conducting third-party audits of Tier-1 agricultural aggregators; mapping Tier-2 and Tier-3 suppliers for high-risk commodities.
- Grievance mechanism: establishing an accessible grievance mechanism via a multilingual helpline, and providing capacity building to suppliers on labour rights.
- Labour: conducting a living wage gap analysis benchmarking against credible methodologies for ALL locations (the mitigation text then truncates at 'Ensuring compliance with').
- Procurement profile disclosed as ESG context: direct procurement from MSMEs and small producers was 24% per FY25 and 25% per FY26.
- STATED ABSENCE (a real finding, not silence): 'The Company does not have any formal supplier awareness program as of now, though the Company is in process of formally adopting a supplier engagement program which includes the awareness on the principles of BRSR and will be reporting the same from next financial year.' [BACK-FILLED with provenance from the sibling capex_expansion bundle's BRSR extract.]
- STATED ABSENCE: green R&D intensity reported as 0% of total R&D investments in both FY 2025-26 and FY 2024-25, against green capex of 16.53% (FY26) and 36.05% (FY25) of total capex, on a basis the Company states it re-assessed after previously reporting these metrics as Zero. [BACK-FILLED with provenance from the sibling capex_expansion bundle.]
- STATED ABSENCE: 'During the reporting period, no instances of fines, penalties, or actions by regulatory or judicial authorities related to corruption or conflict of interest were identified', supported by the Code of Conduct, anti-corruption measures and internal controls, with regular monitoring and awareness initiatives. [BACK-FILLED with provenance from the sibling capex_expansion bundle's BRSR extract.]
- Governance of conflicts of interest: a Board-approved Policy on Related Party Transactions (recommended by the Audit Committee) identifies, deals with and manages conflicts of interest with related parties; all RPTs are at arm's length and subject to prior approval/ratification of the Audit Committee, and 'There were no materially significant transactions during the year that could have resulted in a conflict of interest.' [BACK-FILLED with provenance from the sibling capex_expansion / governance_entities bundles.]
- DATA-QUALITY CAVEAT on this whole BRSR materiality table: it arrives with its opening line truncated ('ease indicate material r...') and its final row (row 8, Climate Change) cut off mid-phrase at 'UN ESC', so row 8's mitigation and implications are absent. Columns for rows 3, 5 and 7 are scrambled across page breaks, with mitigation and implications cells appearing out of order and after subsequent rows; row 7's rationale ends mid-sentence at 'Labour'. No numeric ESG target, baseline value, target year or intensity metric appears anywhere in the table — every commitment is directional only.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: The Company discloses no dedicated capex chapter and no project-wise expansion narrative with commissioning timelines. What the routed text supports: (1) TWO NEW MANUFACTURING FACILITIES — the BRSR reporting-boundary note states 'Current reporting boundary for the Company for BRSR does not include manufacturing facilities located at Krishnapatnam, Telangana and Alwar, Rajasthan. As they came into operation mid-year, the Company will be reporting key disclosure for these two facilities from next financial year.' This is the only concrete FY'26 capacity-addition event in the annual report; no capacity quantum (MT/TPD), no commissioning date and no project cost are stated for either site. [BACK-FILLED with provenance from the sibling profile bundle's BRSR Section A extract — the BRSR text routed into THIS capex bundle begins mid-way through Principle 1 and does not carry the boundary note.] Note the location as printed: 'Krishnapatnam, Telangana' — Krishnapatnam is commonly located in Andhra Pradesh, but the state is reproduced exactly as printed and NOT corrected. (2) CAPACITY RE-PIVOT — in Chocolates, 'As aligned with the Board in FY'25, the Company has ceased further investments in this category. Over time, the Board will also evaluate opportunities to either divest or re-pivot capacities within this segment.' (3) CAPITAL-ALLOCATION INTENT — following the Del Monte Foods Private Limited acquisition the Company is 'strengthening its cash position to capitalize on identified high-potential opportunities across both organic and inorganic avenues. These include investments in capacity expansion as viable, brand development, product innovation, and selective strategic acquisitions', and retains earnings (no FY26 dividend) to 'fund its expansion plans'. (4) DISTRIBUTION / CHANNEL BUILD-OUT (the asset-light form of expansion here) — direct retail coverage maintained at 493,000 outlets across India, a sales force automation tool now covering approx 3,75,000 outlets tracked on a mobile app, continued scale-up in e-commerce and quick commerce, expanded IPC pack sizes launched in FY'26, and new chocolate / high-protein Spreads variants and multiple new Peanut butter variants launched in the last 6 months. (5) GREEN CAPEX INTENSITY (BRSR Principle 2, Essential Indicator 1 — percentage of R&D and capex investments in specific technologies to improve environmental and social impacts, as a share of total R&D and capex): R&D 0% in FY 2025-26 and 0% in FY 2024-25; Capex 16.53% in FY 2025-26 and 36.05% in FY 2024-25; the 'Details of improvements in environmental and social impacts' column reads NA for both rows. A footnote flags a RESTATEMENT of basis: '** We have identified R&D and CAPEX investments that demonstrate Company's efforts to improve environmental and social impacts of our products. We had earlier reported these metrics as Zero. However, after re-assessment of the investments we have estimated the same.' These are percentages, not rupee quanta, so they are recorded here and NOT in capex_disclosed. (6) The Company was renamed during the period and is printed throughout as 'Sundrop Brands Limited (Formerly Known as Agro Tech Foods Limited)'; the consolidated group was also restructured by the acquisition of 100% of Del Monte Foods Private Limited on February 6, 2025 (acquisition date), with Del Monte Foods India (North) Private Limited as a step-down wholly owned subsidiary. --- NAMED DISCLOSURE DEFECTS (figures deliberately NOT promoted into capex_disclosed): both named blocks in this bundle arrive WITHOUT readable period dates, so no figure can be assigned to a year without guessing. Reproduced verbatim: [A] '=== NAMED DISCLOSURE — CAPITAL COMMITMENTS ===  [page 242] (All amounts are in ` crores, except share data and where otherwise stated) | As at  /  Estimated amount of contracts remaining to be executed on capital  /  3.03 ... 2.76'. The column header is the bare fragment 'As at' with NO date, and the line-item label itself is truncated mid-phrase ('...remaining to be executed on capital' — the customary continuation 'account and not provided for' is missing). Two figures are printed (3.03 and 2.76) with nothing in the block stating which belongs to 31 March 2026 and which to the comparative. [B] '=== NAMED DISCLOSURE — SEGMENT CAPITAL EXPENDITURE ===  [page 177] (All amounts are in ` crores, except share data and where otherwise stated) | For the year ended | As at  /  Capital expenditure  /  0.66 ... 1.01' and an IDENTICAL second block '[page 248] ... Capital expenditure 0.66 ... 1.01'. Same defect — headers 'For the year ended' and 'As at' carry no dates. Additionally FLAGGED AS IMPLAUSIBLE AS A COMPANY TOTAL: a capital expenditure of 0.66 crores cannot be reconciled with a year in which two manufacturing facilities at Krishnapatnam and Alwar came into operation; the row is almost certainly a single segment's column rather than the entity total, and the block gives no segment label to confirm which. The unit line ('` crores') IS readable in every block and is recorded verbatim here; only the dates and segment labels are missing.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- The Indian FMCG sector is described as remaining on a structurally strong growth trajectory, supported by rising disposable incomes, an expanding middle class, improving rural demand and the rapid scale-up of digital & quick commerce channels.
- Industry cycle framing: the FMCG industry experienced cost-led pressures and demand moderation through FY'24; recovery trends strengthened through FY'25 and continued into FY'26 with improving consumption sentiment.
- The Indian Foods market is stated to present a significant long-term growth opportunity driven by favorable demographics, rising incomes and increasing penetration across under-developed categories.
- The Company's presence in relatively low-penetration food segments is stated to provide a strong runway for sustained growth in both revenue and profitability.
- The Indian packaged food industry is said to offer significant headroom within the Company's core categories, to be captured by penetration into new households and increased consumption among existing households.
- Mix shift as a margin lever: the Foods portfolio accounted for 60% of revenue and 70% of Gross Margin in FY'26, described as reflecting improving quality of earnings and a strategic shift towards higher-margin categories.
- E-commerce is called out as the fast-growing channel — Ready to Cook snacks grew 52% in E-commerce versus 9% category value growth; larger IPC pack sizes now contribute over 10% of IPC sales in e-commerce.
- Advertising and Promotion (A&P) expenditure increased by 25% during the year, stated as commitment to brand equity, consumer acquisition and growth across channels.
- Headwind: the recent uptick in crude-linked input costs is flagged as a potential headwind to margins going forward; crude sunflower oil prices rose by over 10% during FY'26.
- Headwind: inflationary pressures in key raw materials have the potential to impact margins and necessitate price increases, which may in turn affect consumption; the Edible Oils segment retains sensitivity for overall profitability even though its portfolio contribution has reduced over time.
- Headwind: heightened competitive intensity in Spreads and Dips, particularly in Organised and Standalone Modern Trade, with sustained pricing pressure and rapid scale-up of new-age brands offering premium high-protein and chocolate variants.
- Offsetting lever: brands are stated to have strong equity and pricing power, enabling protection of realisation through optimised price increases and trade scheme reductions (back-filled from the profile bundle — this paragraph falls after this bundle's truncation point).
- Category-level FY'26 operating commentary given as the base for outlook: RTC Snacks value growth 9%; RTE Snacks volume +21% / value +35% with Gross Margins expanded by 4 times; Breakfast Cereals volume +1% / value +8% with Gross Margins up over 5.5 times; Spreads & Dips volume -10% / value -7%; Chocolates volume -70% / value -67% and now insignificant to total business; Premium Staples-Oils volume +2% / value +16% largely price-driven with category gross margins down 9%; Mass Edible Oils/Staples volume -21% / revenue -6%; Plain Oats value growth 16%.
- Breakfast Cereals profitability improvement is stated to position the Company to drive distribution-led growth for that category in the years ahead.

deepdive.thesis: Sundrop Brands delivered strong 11% Q4 consolidated revenue growth and EBITDA margin expansion to 7.2% driven by volume-led category growth and cost efficiencies, with a clear path to 100-200 bps synergy gains via ERP integration and optimized distribution by FY28 — what matters is the transition from standalone growth to integrated scale with sustainable profitability.

risks.note: MD&A: 'the business continues to remain exposed to volatility in input costs, particularly within the Edible Oils segment.' Crude sunflower oil prices rose by over 10% during FY'26 and management flags that 'The recent uptick in crude-linked input costs poses a potential headwind to margins going forward.' Explicitly structural rather than transient: 'While the contribution of the Edible Oils business to the overall portfolio has reduced over time, it continues to have a sensitivity for the Company's overall profitability.' Mitigation stated as portfolio diversification, calibrated pricing actions and continued scale-up of the higher-margin Foods business.
risks.risk: Input-cost volatility, concentrated in Edible Oils

risks.note: MD&A: 'Inflationary pressures in key raw materials have the potential to impact margins and necessitate price increases, which may in turn affect consumption.' Demonstrated in-year rather than hypothetical: in Premium Staples the Company 'successfully passed on the increase in input costs' but 'higher pricing had an impact on volumes during the year' (volume +2% against value +16%, largely price-driven), and category gross margins still declined 9%.
risks.risk: Price-elasticity of demand — passing on inflation costs volume

risks.note: MD&A: heightened competitive intensity during FY'26 'particularly in Organised and Standalone Modern Trade (SAMT), with sustained pricing pressure', intensified by 'the entry and rapid scale-up of new-age brands, which gained share across e-commerce and modern trade channels through premium offerings such as high-protein and chocolate variants.' The category registered a volume decline of 10% and a value decline of 7% during the year — the only core Foods category in outright decline other than the deliberately-exited Chocolates.
risks.risk: Competitive intensity and share loss in Spreads & Dips

risks.note: BRSR material-issues table, row 1 (classified RISK): 'Sundrop Brands' operates six manufacturing plants across climate-vulnerable regions. Processing-intensive operations generate significant Scope 1 and 2 emissions. BRSR Core reasonable assurance became mandatory for top 1,000 companies in FY25-26, requiring verified GHG accounting. India's net-zero 2070 commitment creates investor scrutiny on decarbonization. Failure to demonstrate emission reduction could impact access to green financing.' Stated negative implications: transition costs for renewable installations, efficiency upgrades and carbon accounting systems, plus 'Potential carbon tax liability if pricing mechanisms implemented.'
risks.risk: GHG emissions and climate-transition exposure across a processing-intensive plant base

risks.note: BRSR row 3 (RISK): 'Sundrop Brands' plants in Gujarat, Telangana, and UP face acute water stress. Gujarat's central-east region experiences severe drought. Telangana's groundwater crisis deepens—study by Telangana Rythu Commission and University of Hyderabad (January 2026) warns of Day Zero threat by 2034 with groundwater levels projected to decline 68%. Edible oil refining and food processing are water-intensive. Communities surrounding plants compete for scarce groundwater. Regulatory authorities tightened abstraction permits in FY25-26.' Stated negative implication includes 'Risk of production shutdowns if permits suspended' plus capital investment for ZLD systems, water recycling infrastructure and rainwater harvesting.
risks.risk: Acute water stress at plant locations — licence-to-operate and shutdown risk

risks.note: BRSR row 5 (RISK): 'Six facilities with diverse processes—oil refining at high temperatures, automated packaging, chemical handling—expose workers to heat stress, machinery accidents, and chemical hazards. Summer 2025 saw record temperatures in Gujarat and Telangana. Assam plant faces recurring monsoon floods. OSH Code implementation progresses at state level, raising compliance standards. BRSR Core mandates LTIFR disclosure with reasonable assurance.' Stated negatives include potential liabilities from workplace accidents including compensation and legal costs.
risks.risk: Employee health & safety across high-temperature and chemical-handling operations

risks.note: BRSR row 6 (RISK): 'Sundrop Brands' procures from MSMEs and small producers (24% direct procurement per FY25 and 25% per FY26), creating exposure to labour rights risks in agricultural supply chains—particularly peanut sourcing in Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh. Seasonal agricultural workers from marginalized communities face wage violations and unsafe conditions. India's ILO convention ratification and emerging global supply chain due diligence standards create rising scrutiny. Inadequate grievance mechanisms could trigger ESG index exclusions.' Compounding this, the Company states it has no formal supplier awareness programme yet (see esg list) — a supplier-oversight gap against an identified supply-chain risk.
risks.risk: Human-rights and labour-rights exposure in an MSME/smallholder agricultural supply chain

risks.note: BRSR row 7 (RISK): 'Food processing faces scrutiny over fair wages, working hours during peak seasons, and freedom of association. Telangana and Gujarat plants face unionization pressures. Gender diversity remains low in manufacturing. Labour' — the rationale cell TRUNCATES mid-sentence at the word 'Labour' and its mitigation column is split across a page break, surviving only as 'Conducting living wage gap analysis benchmarking against credible methodologies for all locations. Ensuring compliance with'. Stated negatives: incremental cost for wage-gap bridging, enhanced benefits and HR system upgrades.
risks.risk: Labour practices — wages, peak-season hours, unionisation and low gender diversity
